- Know what a `classes` and object oriented programming

:::

## Classes

**Classes** can be seen as fancy structs which are equipped with

- constructors that take care of initialization
- destructors that take care of deletion
- (copy) operations
- functions that operate on the data (methods)
- hierarchies
- protection of variables and functions
- $\ldots$

## Classes - Syntax


```{.cpp}
class class_name{
private:
  // private variables and functions
public:
  // public variables and functions
};
``` 

Example:
```{.cpp}
class Entry {
private:
  long _data;
  Entry *_next;
  Entry *_previous;

public:
  Entry(long data) : _data(data) {}
};
```


In C++ the only difference between `struct` and `class` is whether data is `public` or `private` by default.  

## Classes - Functions 1/2
```{.cpp}
class Entry {
private:
  long _data;
  Entry *_next;
  Entry *_previous;

public:
  Entry(long data) : _data(data) {}
  void Print() { std::cout << _data << std::endl; }
};

Entry first(2);
first.print();
```

## Classes - Functions 2/2

```{.cpp}
class Entry {
private:
  long _data;
  Entry *_next;
  Entry *_previous;

public:
  Entry(long data) : _data(data) {}
  void Print();
};

void Entry::Print() { std::cout << _data << std::endl; }
```

## Classes - private and public

```{.cpp}
#include <iostream>

class Entry {
private:
  long _data;
  Entry *_next;
  Entry *_previous;

public:
  long _publicData;
  Entry(long data) : _data(data), _publicData(data) {}
};

Entry first(2);
std::cout << first._data;
std::cout << first._publicData;
```

- `private` data/functions are protected from modification
- `public` data/functions are accessible 
- note that the `Print` function _can_ access `private` data 

## The constructor 1/2

- Every class has a constructor, i.e., a function which is called when an object is created.

```{.cpp}
class Entry{
    ...
public:
    Entry(long data);
};

Entry::Entry(long data)
    : _data(data), _publicData(data), _next(0), _previous(0) {
  std::cout << "Constructor called." << std::endl;
}
```

What happens if we create an object `Entry tmp`?

## The constructor 2/2

```{.cpp}
class Entry{
    ...
public:
    Entry(double data);
private:
    Entry(){}
};
```

- Making the default constructor private will remove the option to call it.




## Data management 1/2

```{.cpp}
class Entry {
  double *_data;

public:
  Entry(double data) : _data(new double) { *_data = data; }
};

int main() {
  if (true)
    Entry tmp(1);
  return 0;
}
``` 

- What behaviour do you expect?
- Dynamic memory will not be deleted by default. This has to be done via the destructor.

## Data management
```{.cpp}
class Entry {
  double *_data;

public:
  Entry(double data) : _data(new double) { *_data = data; }
  ~Entry() { delete _data; }
};

int main() {
  if (true)
    Entry tmp(1);
  return 0;
}
``` 

- What behaviour do you expect?
- Dynamic memory will not be deleted by default. This has to be done via the destructor.
- Usually an object which allocates dynamic memory is responsible for deallocating it.


## Do I need a destructor?
```{.cpp}
class Entry {
  double *_data;

public:
  Entry(double data) : _data(NULL) {
    _data = new double[10];
    _data[0] = data;
  }
};

int main() {
  double *data = new double;
  Entry tmp(*data);
  delete data;
  return 0;
}

```

## What does this code do? 1/8
```{.cpp}
class Entry {
  double *_data;

public:
  Entry(double data) : _data(&data) {}
  ~Entry() { delete data; }
};

int main() {
  double *data = new double;
  Entry tmp(data);
  delete data;
  return 0;
}
```

## What was the problem?

- Class undefined when used in function [(forward declaration can help)]{style="color:green"}
- Function accessed private data [(declare as friend)]{style="color:green"}

**Data protection:**

- Ensure that data is not manipulated.
- Think of all the errors we generated by passing a pointer to the constructor.

## Copy constructor 2/3

- Function `foo` creates a new object `aFoo` and copies all values from `a`.
- We did not specify how this new class `A` is copied!
- By default all variables are simply copied. I.e., `aFoo._d = a._d`.
- `aFoo` is deallocated when leaving function (static memory!)
- Destructor of `aFoo` deallocates `aFoo._d` and thereby `a._d`.
- Good thing we understand pointers ;)

**Way out:** Define our own copy constructor.

##  Summary
Classes can be used to **group data and operations** on them.

- More in object oriented programming
- This helps to structure code.

But if dynamic memory is used there can be issues.

- Managed via constructors and destructors.
- This is how std::vector is implemented.

For your own code **consider using `std::vector` and other higher-level classes that have allocation and deallocation already figured out** .
